GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Advance Directives &:
What & Why

Advance care planning is the process by which a person with capacity records their wishes for future care and treatment, so that if they later lose capacity, their voice still guides decisions. It matters because it is where medical law meets end-of-life practice — in geriatrics, oncology, and progressive disease you constantly manage patients whose capacity may fail, and you need to know which documents are legally binding and which are advisory, and who gets to decide. The whole area hangs off the Mental Capacity Act 2005 — the same statute that governs adult consent generally.

The framing that matters: everything sorts into a hierarchy of legal force. At the top sits a document that binds you like a contemporaneous refusal by a competent patient (the Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment); below it, documents that appoint a decision-maker (Lasting Power of Attorney); and at the bottom, statements that are influential but not binding (advance statements).
The Decisive Fork — Does the Person Currently Have Capacity?
Has capacity nowLacks capacity now
Who decidesThe patient — contemporaneous consent/refusal always governsFollow the hierarchy below
Planning toolsCan make an Advance Decision, Lasting Power of Attorney, advance statementThese now come into force
Key ruleA capacitous patient can refuse any treatment, even life-saving, for any/no reasonDecisions made for them, per the Act
Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and presumed unless shown otherwise (Mental Capacity Act principle 1). An advance document only becomes relevant when capacity for that specific decision is lost.
The Mental Capacity Act Foundation — 5 Statutory Principles
  • Presume capacity unless established otherwise
  • Support the person to make their own decision (all practicable help) before deeming them unable
  • An unwise decision ≠ lack of capacity
  • Act in the person’s best interests if they lack capacity
  • Choose the least restrictive option
Capacity test (2-stage): (1) is there an impairment of mind/brain? (2) does it mean they can’t understand, retain, weigh, or communicate the decision?
The Hierarchy of End-of-Life Documents
📷 Image placeholder — Ladder of legal force — a valid/applicable ADRT (binding refusal) > Health & Welfare LPA / court-appointed deputy > advance statement (advisory only), with the life-sustaining ADRT formalities at the top rung
1. Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) — legally binding
  • Also called a “living will”. Lets an adult refuse specified treatments in advance, to apply if they later lose capacity
  • A valid and applicable Advance Decision is legally binding — the same force as a contemporaneous refusal by a competent patient; overriding it risks criminal (battery) or civil liability
  • It can ONLY refuse treatment — never demand/request a specific treatment, and never anything unlawful (euthanasia/assisted dying are illegal in the UK). It cannot refuse basic care (warmth, hygiene, oral food/fluids) or symptom relief
  • Validity: person was ≥18 and had capacity when making it; specifies the treatment refused + circumstances; not withdrawn/contradicted; circumstances not materially different
  • To refuse LIFE-SUSTAINING treatment, extra formalities: it must be in writing, signed, witnessed, and state it applies “even if life is at risk” (the single most-tested detail). If these aren’t met it’s not binding, but still counts as evidence of wishes
2. Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) — appoints a decision-maker
  • Lets a person (the donor) appoint an attorney to decide if they lose capacity. Two types: Health & Welfare and Property & Financial Affairs
  • Only the Health & Welfare LPA covers medical treatment — usable only once the donor lacks capacity
  • Covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated on the LPA; must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian
  • The attorney acts in the donor’s best interests — cannot demand treatment clinicians judge inappropriate, and cannot consent to something a valid later ADRT already refused
3. Advance Statement — influential, NOT binding
  • A written/verbal statement of wishes, preferences, values, beliefs (e.g. “I’d prefer to die at home”, religious wishes, who to involve)
  • Not legally binding, but must be taken into account in any best-interests decision
The Interaction Rule (high-yield)
ADRT vs LPA — the later document wins: an LPA made after an ADRT (same treatment) can override it; an ADRT made after an LPA takes precedence over the attorney. A valid, applicable ADRT overrides the best-interests provision AND the Court of Protection (the court can only rule on whether it’s valid/applicable).

The order of authority when capacity is lost: valid applicable ADRT (refusals) → Health & Welfare LPA / court-appointed deputy → best-interests decision by the clinical team (taking advance statements, family views, and an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) where required into account). Family/next-of-kin are consulted but cannot consent or refuse unless they hold LPA.

CPR Decisions — DNACPR and ReSPECT
  • DNACPR (“Do Not Attempt CPR”) — a clinical decision recorded in the notes that CPR should not be attempted if the heart/breathing stops. Specific to CPR only; does not affect any other treatment
  • DNACPR is a clinical decision, not the patient’s to demand — but there is a legal duty to consult the patient (or, if they lack capacity, those close to them). The Tracey judgment (2014) established that a patient must be informed and involved unless doing so would cause them physical or psychological harm
  • ReSPECT (Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment) — increasingly replaces standalone DNACPR forms: a broader emergency care plan recording recommendations for CPR and the wider ceiling of treatment (admission, ICU, ventilation). It is a recommendation/summary, not itself legally binding (unlike an ADRT)
Putting It Together — Worked Logic
📷 Image placeholder — Decision flow for the incapacitated patient — valid applicable ADRT? → registered H&W LPA with life-sustaining authority? → best-interests decision by the team (consult family/advance statement/IMCA); family inform but do not decide
An unconscious 82-year-old arrives; family say “she wouldn’t want to be kept alive on machines.” → First, is there a valid, applicable ADRT refusing this treatment (written/signed/witnessed + “even if life at risk”)? If yes → follow it, it’s binding. → If no ADRT, is there a registered Health & Welfare LPA with authority over life-sustaining treatment? → the attorney decides in her best interests. → If neither → the clinical team makes a best-interests decision, consulting family (who inform but don’t decide), any advance statement, and an IMCA if no one is available. Family’s recollection is evidence, not authority.
Exam Pearls
Foundation
Everything sits under the Mental Capacity Act 2005; capacity is presumed, decision-specific, and an unwise choice isn’t incapacity.
ADRT
Legally binding refusal (same force as a competent patient’s refusal); can only REFUSE, never demand; can’t cover basic care or request euthanasia (illegal in UK).
ADRT + life-sustaining
Must be WRITTEN, SIGNED, WITNESSED + state “even if life is at risk.”
LPA
Health & Welfare LPA appoints an attorney (best interests); covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated; must be registered (Office of the Public Guardian).
Advance statement
Wishes/preferences — NOT binding, but must be considered.
Later document wins
LPA after ADRT can override it; ADRT after LPA overrides the attorney. A valid applicable ADRT overrides best interests AND the Court of Protection.
Family
Next-of-kin cannot consent or refuse for an adult unless they hold LPA — they are consulted.
CPR
DNACPR = CPR only, clinical decision, but must involve the patient (Tracey judgment). ReSPECT = broader emergency care plan/recommendation, not itself binding. No decision-maker + serious decision → appoint an IMCA.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Benign Paroxysmal Po:
What & Why

BPPV is recurrent, brief episodes of vertigo triggered by head movement, caused by displaced otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) in the semicircular canals. It matters because it is the single commonest cause of vertigo, a big contributor to falls in the elderly, and — best of all — it’s mechanically curable at the bedside with a repositioning manoeuvre, needing no drugs and no imaging in a typical case.

The framing that matters: vertigo splits into peripheral vs central, and BPPV is the archetypal benign peripheral cause. Its whole identity is a triad: positional trigger + very short duration (seconds) + NO hearing loss or tinnitus. That triad separates it from its peripheral cousins (Ménière’s has hearing loss/tinnitus; vestibular neuronitis is constant and prolonged) and from the dangerous central mimics (stroke, tumour, multiple sclerosis).
The Pathophysiology
  • Otoconia (calcium-carbonate crystals) normally sit in the utricle. In BPPV they dislodge into a semicircular canal — most often the posterior canal (~85–90%)
  • When the head moves, the loose crystals move the endolymph abnormally, giving the brain a false signal of rotation → vertigo + nystagmus
  • This is canalithiasis (crystals free in the canal)
  • Causes/associations: usually idiopathic; also head trauma, ageing, prolonged bed rest, and following vestibular neuronitis/labyrinthitis
The Decisive Fork — Peripheral (BPPV) or Central?

The safety-critical distinction — you must not miss a posterior-circulation stroke masquerading as vertigo:

FeatureBPPV (peripheral)Central (stroke/tumour/multiple sclerosis)
OnsetSudden, positionalGradual (except stroke: sudden)
DurationSeconds (20–60 s), settles when stillPersistent
TriggerHead movement (rolling in bed, looking up)Not purely positional
Hearing loss/tinnitusNoneUsually none, but variable
NystagmusUpbeating-torsional (toward the affected ear), fatigable, with latencyVertical / bidirectional / direction-changing, non-fatiguing
Neuro signsNoneAtaxia, diplopia, dysarthria, limb/cranial-nerve signs
HINTS examPeripheral patternCentral pattern
Red flags for a central cause (→ urgent imaging/stroke pathway): vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, other neurological signs, inability to stand/walk, severe headache, sudden persistent vertigo.
Clinical Features
  • Vertigo triggered by head movements — classically turning over in bed, lying down, looking up (“top-shelf vertigo”), bending forward
  • Very brief — episodes last ~20–60 seconds and settle if the head is kept still
  • Recurrent episodes
  • NO hearing loss and NO tinnitus (the key discriminator from Ménière’s and labyrinthitis)
  • No spontaneous vertigo at rest; between episodes the patient is well (sometimes residual unsteadiness/nausea)
Investigations — Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre
📷 Image placeholder — Dix-Hallpike — head turned 45° to the tested side, laid back rapidly with the head hanging 20–30° below the couch; watch for latent, transient, fatiguable upbeating-torsional nystagmus toward the lower ear
  • Dix-Hallpike is the gold-standard diagnostic test (“D for Diagnosis”)
  • Method: patient sits upright with head turned 45° toward the side being tested; rapidly lie them back so the head hangs ~20–30° below the couch edge; keep the head there and watch the eyes for up to ~30–60 s
  • Positive result: after a brief latency (a few seconds), rotatory (torsional) nystagmus toward the affected (lower) ear + the patient’s vertigo; it is fatigable (lessens on repeat) — latency and fatigability point away from a central cause
  • Caution/contraindications: neck pathology, recent neck/spinal injury, carotid disease — do a modified version or avoid
  • No imaging needed for typical BPPV; reserve MRI for atypical features or central red flags
  • Horizontal-canal BPPV (less common) is diagnosed with the supine roll test, not Dix-Hallpike
Management — Epley Manoeuvre
📷 Image placeholder — Epley canalith-repositioning for right posterior-canal BPPV — the four sequential head/body positions (each held ~30 s) that roll otoconia back into the utricle
First-line = the Epley manoeuvre (a canalith repositioning procedure — “E for treatment”): a sequence of head positions that rolls the otoconia out of the posterior canal back into the utricle. Highly effective — often works after 1–2 attempts (Cochrane-supported).
Epley sequence
  • Start as for Dix-Hallpike → rotate head 90° to the opposite side
  • Roll onto that side so the head turns a further 90° (now facing the floor)
  • Sit up sideways → return head to midline with neck flexed
  • Hold each position ~30 s until nystagmus/dizziness settles
  • Brandt-Daroff exercises — patient-performed home exercises; an option if Epley isn’t available/tolerated or for residual symptoms (less effective than Epley)
  • Self-limiting: most cases resolve within weeks to ~6 months even untreated, but repositioning speeds resolution dramatically
  • Medication is NOT recommended — vestibular sedatives/antihistamines (betahistine, prochlorperazine, cinnarizine) have little benefit in BPPV and may delay central compensation; they don’t address the mechanical cause (contrast with vestibular neuronitis, where short-term prochlorperazine is used)
  • Refer to ENT/balance clinic if: diagnosis uncertain, atypical/central features, symptoms persist despite repeated repositioning, or frequent recurrence. Surgery (posterior-canal occlusion) is a last resort for intractable cases
  • Safety: counsel on fall risk, driving when dizzy, and occupational hazards; recurrence is common (~50% over years)
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest cause of vertigo; displaced otoconia (canalithiasis) in the semicircular canal (usually posterior).
Triad
Positional trigger + very brief (seconds, 20–60 s) + NO hearing loss/tinnitus. Classic trigger: rolling over in bed / looking up.
Diagnosis
Dix-Hallpike → latency, then rotatory nystagmus to the affected ear, fatigable (D for Diagnosis).
Treatment
Epley (canalith repositioning) manoeuvre — first-line, curative (E for treatment); Brandt-Daroff at home.
Medication
Vestibular sedatives are NOT recommended in BPPV (unlike vestibular neuronitis).
Course
Self-limiting over weeks–6 months; no imaging in typical cases.
Central red flags
Vertical/direction-changing nystagmus, neuro signs, persistent vertigo, can’t walk → think posterior-circulation stroke, use HINTS, image.
Differentials
Ménière’s (vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + fullness), vestibular neuronitis (constant, prolonged, post-viral, no hearing loss), labyrinthitis (like neuronitis but with hearing loss).
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Comprehensive Geriat:
What & Why

CGA is a multidimensional, multidisciplinary diagnostic and therapeutic process that assesses an older person’s medical, functional, psychological, and social capabilities and problems, in order to build a coordinated, integrated plan for treatment and follow-up. It matters because it is the single defining tool of geriatric medicine — the structured answer to the problem that older people with frailty and multimorbidity don’t fit the ‘one patient, one diagnosis’ model. A standard disease-focused clerking misses the falls, the cognition, the polypharmacy, the isolation — CGA catches all of it at once, and it has hard outcome evidence behind it.

The framing that matters: CGA is not a questionnaire or a score — it’s a process. It rests on two pillars: it is multidimensional (assesses several domains, not just the presenting complaint) and multidisciplinary (delivered by a team, not one doctor). The output is a problem list and a coordinated management plan, revisited iteratively. If you remember nothing else: holistic + team-based + iterative plan.
Why It Exists — the Evidence
Guideline-verified — Cochrane / British Geriatrics Society.
  • Older people with moderate–severe frailty admitted as an emergency who receive CGA are more likely to be alive and living in their own home at follow-up (and less likely to be institutionalised)
  • Benefits include reduced institutionalisation, better functional outcomes, and — operationally — shorter length of stay and fewer readmissions
  • Works across settings: acute “front-door” frailty units, inpatient wards, community, and home-based CGA
The Organising Principle — the Domains
📷 Image placeholder — The six CGA domains — physical/medical, psychological, functional, social, environmental, future wishes — each with an anchor tool (STOPP/START, 4AT/GDS, Barthel/TUG, social work, OT home assessment, ReSPECT)

CGA is structured around a set of domains — the British Geriatrics Society framework uses physical, psychological, functional, social, environmental, and future wishes. This is the scaffold to memorise:

DomainWhat it coversExample tools/actions
Physical / MedicalComorbidities/multimorbidity, frailty syndromes (falls, immobility, incontinence, delirium), medication review / polypharmacy, continence, nutrition, pain, sensory (vision/hearing), skinProblem list; STOPP/START review; bloods; nutrition (MUST)
PsychologicalCognition (dementia, delirium), mood (depression, anxiety), mental capacityAMTS / MoCA / MMSE / 4AT (delirium); Geriatric Depression Scale
FunctionalBasic ADLs (washing, dressing, feeding, transfers) and IADLs (cooking, shopping, finances, medications), mobility, balance, gaitBarthel Index; Timed Up-and-Go; gait/balance
SocialCare/support network, informal carers (and carer strain), formal care package, finances, safeguardingSocial work input; care needs assessment
EnvironmentalHome setup, falls hazards, aids/adaptations, accessOccupational-therapy home assessment
Future wishesAdvance care planning, ADRT/LPA, ceilings of treatment, ReSPECT/DNACPR, preferred place of careAdvance-care-planning conversation
The Multidisciplinary Team

CGA is never one clinician. Core members and roles:

  • Geriatrician / medical lead — overarching clinical assessment and plan
  • Nurses — monitoring, skin/nutrition/continence, holistic care
  • Physiotherapist — mobility, balance, falls, strength
  • Occupational therapist — function, ADLs, home/environment assessment, aids/adaptations
  • Pharmacist — medication optimisation and polypharmacy review
  • Dietitian — nutrition; SALT — swallow/communication
  • Social worker / care coordinator — social needs, care packages, safeguarding, discharge
  • Plus mental health links, and crucially the patient and their family/carers at the centre
The CGA Process — How It Actually Runs
📷 Image placeholder — The five-step CGA loop — identify (frailty screen) → multidimensional assessment → MDT synthesis → coordinated goal-based plan → implement and iterate
The five steps
  • Identify the right patients — older people with frailty and multimorbidity (screen with a frailty tool, e.g. Clinical Frailty Scale, PRISMA-7, or gait speed). Targeted at those who benefit most — not every older patient
  • Multidimensional assessment across the domains above, each team member contributing
  • MDT meeting — synthesise into a shared problem list
  • Coordinated management/care plan with clear goals (often patient-centred functional goals, not just disease targets)
  • Implement, then review and iterate — with defined follow-up
Where CGA Is Delivered
  • Acute hospital / “front-door” frailty units, emergency department, Same Day Emergency Care — urgent CGA to avoid unnecessary admission and deconditioning
  • Inpatient geriatric wards — the classic setting with the strongest evidence
  • Community and home-based — admission-avoidance and rehabilitation
  • Perioperative (e.g. POPS — proactive care of older people undergoing surgery) and oncology (assessing fitness for treatment)
Key Linked Concepts
  • Frailty — the target population; a state of reduced physiological reserve and vulnerability to stressors
  • The “geriatric giants” / frailty syndromes — falls, immobility, delirium/confusion, incontinence, iatrogenic harm (polypharmacy) — CGA is designed to surface these
  • Deconditioning — the harm of unnecessary bed rest, which urgent CGA aims to prevent
Exam Pearls
What it is
Multidimensional + multidisciplinary diagnostic/therapeutic PROCESS → coordinated care plan for older people with frailty/multimorbidity. It’s a process, not a score.
Domains
Physical/medical, Psychological (cognition + mood), Functional (ADLs/IADLs, mobility), Social, Environmental, Future wishes.
Team
Geriatrician, nurse, physio, occupational therapist, pharmacist, dietitian, SALT, social worker + patient/carers.
Evidence
CGA in admitted frail older people → more likely alive and in their own home, less institutionalisation (Cochrane/British Geriatrics Society).
Target
The frail (Clinical Frailty Scale / gait speed) — not every older patient.
Tools
Function = ADLs (Barthel) and IADLs; cognition = AMTS/MoCA; delirium = 4AT; medication = STOPP/START.
Settings
Acute frailty units, wards, community/home, perioperative (POPS), oncology.
Output
Problem list + patient-centred, coordinated plan, reviewed iteratively.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Delirium:
What & Why

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness, attention, cognition, and perception — an acute confusional state that develops over hours to days and is caused by an underlying physical trigger. It matters because it is one of the “geriatric giants,” it is extremely common in unwell older inpatients, it is a marker of serious illness (roughly doubles mortality and predicts future dementia and institutionalisation), and — crucially — it is often reversible if you find and treat the cause. It is also massively under-recognised, especially the quiet (hypoactive) form.

The framing that matters: delirium is a symptom of something else. It is never a diagnosis you stop at — it’s a flashing light that says “this patient has an acute physical problem, go find it.” The entire management is treat the cause + supportive/environmental care, with drugs a reluctant last resort. The single biggest trap is missing hypoactive delirium because the patient is “quiet and no trouble.”
The Decisive Fork — Delirium or Dementia?
📷 Image placeholder — Delirium vs dementia — onset, course, consciousness, attention, reversibility and hallucinations side by side

Distinguishing acute delirium from chronic dementia is the core diagnostic task (and they coexist — delirium superimposed on dementia):

FeatureDeliriumDementia
OnsetAcute (hours–days)Insidious (months–years)
CourseFluctuating (worse at night — “sundowning”)Stable, slowly progressive
Consciousness/alertnessImpaired / alteredUsually normal (until late)
AttentionMarkedly impaired (the hallmark)Relatively preserved early
ReversibilityUsually reversible (treat cause)Irreversible/progressive
HallucinationsCommon (often visual)Less common (except Lewy body dementia)
If you can’t tell delirium from dementia (or delirium-on-dementia) — treat the delirium first (NICE). A collateral history establishing the baseline is essential.
The Three Motor Subtypes
  • Hyperactive — agitated, restless, aggressive, hallucinations, wandering (the “obvious” one)
  • Hypoactive — withdrawn, quiet, drowsy, slow — the commonest and most dangerous subtype because it’s missed (mistaken for depression, fatigue, or “just dementia”) and has worse outcomes
  • Mixed — fluctuates between the two
Risk Factors

Predisposing: older age, pre-existing dementia/cognitive impairment, frailty, sensory impairment (poor vision/hearing), previous delirium, multimorbidity, polypharmacy. Precipitating: acute illness/infection, surgery (especially hip fracture), new drugs, dehydration, pain, catheterisation, change of environment.

Causes — “PINCH ME”
The screen for the trigger (high-yield mnemonic)
  • P — Pain
  • I — Infection (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis — the classic)
  • N — Nutrition / poor intake
  • C — Constipation (and urinary retention)
  • H — Hydration (dehydration)
  • M — Medication (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, steroids; and withdrawal — alcohol/benzos) and Metabolic (hypo/hypernatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, uraemia, hypoxia, thyroid)
  • E — Environment (unfamiliar surroundings) and Electrolytes

(Also: intracranial causes — stroke, subdural, seizure; urinary retention; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal.)

Assessment & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — The 4AT — Alertness, AMT-4, months-of-year backwards, acute change; score ≥4 = possible delirium
Guideline-verified — NICE CG103.
  • Screen with the 4AT in anyone with indicators of delirium (the recommended UK tool): (1) Alertness, (2) AMT-4 (age, date of birth, place, year), (3) Attention — months of the year backwards, (4) Acute change/fluctuation. Score ≥4 → possible delirium. In ICU/recovery, use CAM-ICU instead
  • Confirm the diagnosis clinically (a competent professional makes the final call) and document it in the notes and GP record
  • Find the cause (targeted to PINCH ME): obs (sepsis screen), bloods (FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, LFTs, TFTs, CRP, magnesium), urinalysis/culture (but don’t over-diagnose UTI — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in the elderly), CXR, ECG, medication review, and consider CT head if focal signs, head injury, or no cause found
  • Collateral history to establish cognitive baseline
Management

1. Treat the underlying cause(s) — the definitive treatment (antibiotics for infection, analgesia for pain, rehydration, relieve constipation/retention, stop the culprit drug, correct electrolytes).

2. Supportive / non-pharmacological care — FIRST-LINE for the delirium itself
  • Reorientation — clocks, calendars, familiar objects, staff introducing themselves, explaining what’s happening
  • Involve family/carers; consistency of staff
  • Optimise environment — good lighting, quiet, promote normal sleep–wake cycle (minimise night-time disturbance)
  • Sensory aids — glasses and hearing aids on
  • Mobilise, hydrate, nutrition, bowels/bladder, avoid catheters/lines where possible, manage pain
  • De-escalation (verbal and non-verbal) for agitation
3. Medication — LAST resort (only if distressed or a risk, AND de-escalation has failed)
  • Short-term haloperidol at the lowest dose, usually ≤1 week; heed the MHRA warning on cardiac (QTc) and neurological effects in older people
  • AVOID antipsychotics (haloperidol) in Parkinson’s disease and dementia with Lewy bodies — severe extrapyramidal reactions. Use a benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam) instead in those patients
  • For alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium → benzodiazepines (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) are first-line, NOT antipsychotics
  • Antipsychotics do not treat or prevent delirium — they only manage severe distress until the cause is corrected; review daily
  • Avoid physical restraint and, where possible, sedation — they worsen delirium and cause harm
Prevention

Multicomponent prevention in at-risk inpatients: orientation, early mobilisation, hydration/nutrition, sleep hygiene, sensory aids, pain control, avoiding constipation, and medication review to avoid deliriogenic drugs. Prevention is more effective than treatment.

Prognosis & Follow-up

Often resolves as the cause is treated, but can take weeks (and sometimes doesn’t fully resolve). An episode is associated with increased mortality, longer admission, functional decline, and later dementia — so follow up and assess for underlying dementia after recovery.

Exam Pearls
What it is
ACUTE, FLUCTUATING disturbance of consciousness + attention + cognition, from an underlying physical cause. It’s a symptom, not a diagnosis.
vs Dementia
Acute onset, fluctuating, impaired consciousness, inattention, reversible (dementia = chronic, stable, alert, irreversible). If unsure → treat delirium first.
Hypoactive
Hypoactive delirium (quiet/drowsy) is commonest and most missed — actively look for it.
Screening
4AT (≥4 = possible delirium); CAM-ICU in critical care.
Causes
PINCH ME — Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication/Metabolic, Environment/Electrolytes. Infection (UTI/pneumonia) and drugs are the big ones.
Management
Treat the cause + non-pharmacological/environmental care FIRST (reorientation, sensory aids, sleep, family, mobilise).
Drugs
Last resort: short-term low-dose haloperidol — but AVOID in Parkinson’s/Lewy body dementia (use lorazepam); benzodiazepines for alcohol/benzo withdrawal. Antipsychotics don’t treat or prevent delirium; avoid restraint/sedation.
Prognosis
Doubles mortality; predicts dementia → follow up cognition after recovery.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Deprivation of Liber:
What & Why

DoLS is the legal framework under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 for lawfully authorising the deprivation of liberty of a person who lacks capacity to consent to their care arrangements, in a hospital or care home, where those arrangements are in their best interests. It matters because you constantly care for people — dementia, delirium, severe learning disability, brain injury — who need to be kept somewhere and stopped from leaving for their own safety, and doing that without legal authorisation breaches their Article 5 (right to liberty) human rights. DoLS makes protective confinement lawful and scrutinised rather than arbitrary.

DoLS remains in force and applies the Cheshire West “acid test”. The framework has long been meant to be replaced by the not-yet-implemented Liberty Protection Safeguards, but that replacement has been repeatedly delayed.
Current Legal Status (2026) — the Moving Parts
The current position
  • DoLS remains the operational process for authorising deprivation of liberty in hospitals and care homes (Court of Protection for other settings). It has not been abolished
  • Liberty Protection Safeguards (LPS) — legislated in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 to replace DoLS with a streamlined, all-settings, age-16+ scheme — has been repeatedly delayed and is still not implemented (a government consultation was announced for 2026)
  • The Cheshire West [2014] UKSC 19 “acid test” remains binding law — it is the determinative test for a deprivation of liberty (see below). When in doubt, use DoLS / Court of Protection processes
The Decisive Question — Is This a Deprivation of Liberty?
📷 Image placeholder — Cheshire West “acid test” — all three limbs: (1) lacks capacity to consent + (2) continuous supervision and control + (3) not free to leave; compliance/benevolence irrelevant

This is the gateway.

The “acid test” (Cheshire West 2014 — the determinative test)
  • A person is deprived of liberty if ALL three: (1) they lack capacity to consent to the arrangements, AND (2) they are under continuous supervision and control, AND (3) they are not free to leave
  • Under the acid test it did NOT matter whether the person was content, whether the arrangements were benevolent/in their best interests, or the purpose — if the three were met, authorisation was needed
Key point — content/benevolence do NOT prevent a deprivation
  • A person who lacks capacity cannot give valid consent to the arrangements — their compliance or contentment is legally irrelevant
  • The benevolent purpose or best-interests nature of the confinement does not stop it being a deprivation
  • If all three limbs of the acid test are met, authorisation is required — “a gilded cage is still a cage” (Cheshire West)
Where the Boundary Sits — Restriction vs Deprivation

A restriction of liberty (e.g. locked ward door for general safety, supervision during activities) is a difference of degree and intensity, not kind, from a deprivation. The more continuous, controlling, and total the arrangements, the more likely it crosses into a deprivation requiring authorisation.

Who and Where
  • DoLS applies to: adults ≥18, who lack capacity to consent to their care/treatment arrangements, in a hospital or care home
  • Other settings (supported living, own home, domestic settings) → deprivation must be authorised by the Court of Protection (a “COPDOL11” application), not DoLS
  • Under-18s / 16–17s → Court of Protection / inherent jurisdiction (not DoLS)
  • If the person is detainable under the Mental Health Act for treatment of a mental disorder and objects, the Mental Health Act may be the correct route instead — the Mental Health Act / Mental Capacity Act interface is a recognised complexity
The DoLS Authorisation Process
📷 Image placeholder — DoLS flow — Managing Authority (hospital/care home) → Supervisory Body (local authority); urgent (self-grant, up to 7 days) + standard (up to 12 months); 6 assessments (age, mental health, mental capacity, best interests, eligibility, no refusals)
  • The “Managing Authority” (the hospital or care home) applies to the “Supervisory Body” (the local authority) for authorisation
  • Urgent authorisation — the managing authority can self-grant for up to 7 days while a standard authorisation is sought
  • Standard authorisation — the supervisory body commissions six assessments: age, mental capacity, mental health, best interests, eligibility (Mental Health Act interface), and no-refusals (checking no valid ADRT/LPA/deputy conflicts)
  • Authorisation is time-limited (up to 12 months) and must be reviewed
  • The person must have a Relevant Person’s Representative and access to an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA); they have a right to challenge the authorisation in the Court of Protection (section 21A)
  • Any deprivation must always be the least restrictive option and in the person’s best interests
How It Fits the Wider Mental Capacity Act Framework

DoLS/LPS sit within the Mental Capacity Act — all five principles apply (presume capacity, support decision-making, unwise decisions aren’t incapacity, best interests, least restrictive). It presupposes a capacity assessment (2-stage test) and a best-interests determination.

Exam Pearls
What it is
Mental Capacity Act 2005 framework to lawfully authorise depriving an incapacitous adult (≥18) of liberty in a HOSPITAL or CARE HOME, protecting Article 5 rights.
Classic acid test
Cheshire West: lacks capacity + continuous supervision & control + not free to leave — and it didn’t matter if the person was content or it was benevolent.
Content ≠ consent
A person lacking capacity cannot validly consent; their compliance/contentment and the benevolence of the arrangements are irrelevant — “a gilded cage is still a cage” (Cheshire West).
Restriction vs deprivation
A matter of degree and intensity.
Process
Managing Authority (hospital/care home) → Supervisory Body (local authority); urgent (7 days) + standard (up to 12 months); 6 assessments; Relevant Person’s Representative + IMCA; challenge via Court of Protection s21A.
Other settings
Own home/supported living → Court of Protection, not DoLS.
LPS
Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 was meant to replace DoLS — still not implemented (2026).
Mental Health Act vs Mental Capacity Act
If detainable and objecting to treatment for a mental disorder, the Mental Health Act may apply instead. Always least restrictive, best interests, within the Mental Capacity Act.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Elder Abuse / Adult:
What & Why

Adult safeguarding is the framework for protecting adults with care and support needs from abuse and neglect — statutorily defined as “protecting an adult’s right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect.” Elder abuse is the commonest context, but the framework covers any adult made vulnerable by their care needs. It matters because these adults are often dependent, isolated, and unable to protect themselves, because the abuse is frequently hidden and by someone trusted (a family carer, partner, or paid staff member), and because — like child protection — every clinician has a duty to recognise concerns and refer, even without proof.

The framing that matters: the pivotal difference from child protection is capacity and autonomy. A child protection concern triggers protective action regardless of the child’s wishes; an adult with capacity has the right to make unwise decisions, including declining help. So adult safeguarding is built around “Making Safeguarding Personal” — working with the adult, respecting their wishes and consent, and only overriding them where they lack capacity or others are at risk. It’s protection with the person, not to them.
The Legal Basis — Section 42, Care Act 2014
📷 Image placeholder — The s42 (Care Act 2014) threshold — all three: care & support needs + experiencing/at risk of abuse or neglect + unable to protect self as a result
The Section 42 duty — the local authority must make a safeguarding enquiry where an adult (ALL three):
  • Has needs for care and support (whether or not the local authority is meeting them), AND
  • Is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect, AND
  • As a result of those care and support needs, is unable to protect themselves against the abuse/neglect or the risk of it

(Where all three aren’t fully met, the local authority may still make proportionate “other” enquiries to promote wellbeing.)

The Six Principles of Adult Safeguarding
Care Act statutory guidance (high-yield)
  • Empowerment — person-led decisions, informed consent (“nothing about me without me”)
  • Prevention — act before harm occurs
  • Proportionality — least intrusive response appropriate to the risk
  • Protection — support and representation for those in greatest need
  • Partnership — local, multi-agency working (communities help prevent/detect/report)
  • Accountability — transparency in delivering safeguarding
“Making Safeguarding Personal” is the overarching approach: outcomes-focused, person-centred — ask the adult what they want to happen, not just impose a process.
Types of Abuse

The Care Act guidance lists 10 categories:

  • Physical — hitting, restraint, misuse of medication
  • Neglect / acts of omission — failure to provide care, food, heating, medication (the commonest form)
  • Psychological / emotional — threats, humiliation, intimidation, coercive control
  • Financial / material — theft, fraud, misuse of money/property, pressure over wills/benefits (especially common in elder abuse)
  • Sexual — any non-consensual sexual act
  • Discriminatory — abuse based on a protected characteristic
  • Organisational / institutional — poor care within a service/care home (neglectful routines, lack of dignity)
  • Domestic abuse — including coercive control by a partner/family member
  • Modern slavery — trafficking, forced labour
  • Self-neglect — neglecting personal hygiene, health, or surroundings (included since the Care Act — a key change; interacts with capacity/hoarding)
Elder Abuse — Recognising It Clinically

Risk factors: cognitive impairment/dementia, physical dependence, social isolation, communication difficulties, a stressed or dependent carer, shared living with the abuser, and carer substance misuse/mental illness.

Red flags (analogous to non-accidental injury, adapted to adults)
  • Injury inconsistent with the explanation, or with unusual pattern/distribution
  • Delayed presentation, or multiple injuries of different ages
  • Unexplained financial changes — new “friends,” missing money, sudden will changes
  • Poor hygiene, malnutrition, dehydration, pressure sores (neglect)
  • Fearfulness, withdrawal, or a carer who answers for the patient / won’t leave the room / is controlling
  • Frequent attendances, missed appointments, medication mismanagement, or behavioural change in the adult
Assessment & the Central Role of Capacity
📷 Image placeholder — Capacity in safeguarding — HAS capacity → consent needed (override only for risk to others/serious crime/coercion/public interest) vs LACKS capacity → best interests + IMCA, refer without consent
  • Assess mental capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2-stage test) for the specific decision (e.g. to accept help, to remain in a situation). This is the hinge of adult safeguarding
  • If the adult HAS capacity: their consent is generally needed to act, and they may decline intervention (right to make unwise decisions). Exceptions to acting without consent: risk to others, a serious crime, undue coercion/duress (so consent isn’t truly free), or a public-interest justification. Continue to offer support
  • If the adult LACKS capacity: act in their best interests, involving family/Independent Mental Capacity Advocate; a referral can be made without their consent
  • Document carefully — history (verbatim where possible), examination/body map, capacity assessment, and the adult’s expressed wishes
Management — What a Clinician Actually Does
The steps
  • Ensure immediate safety (treat injuries, admit if needed, call police if a crime/emergency)
  • Raise a safeguarding concern to the local authority adult safeguarding team — the threshold is reasonable suspicion, not proof; discuss with your safeguarding lead if unsure
  • Respect the adult’s wishes and consent where they have capacity (Making Safeguarding Personal) — but escalate regardless if others are at risk or a serious crime is involved
  • Document contemporaneously and factually; consider others at risk (other residents, dependents, a “person in a position of trust”)
  • Information sharing — seek consent to share, but share without consent where the adult lacks capacity, others are at risk, or it’s in the public interest (proportionate, Data Protection Act 2018/GDPR-compliant)
The Wider Machinery
  • Safeguarding Adults Boards (SABs) — statutory multi-agency boards (local authority, NHS, police) coordinating and overseeing local safeguarding
  • Safeguarding Adults Reviews (SARs) — commissioned by the Board when an adult with care/support needs dies or is seriously harmed and abuse/neglect is known or suspected, to learn lessons (not to allocate blame) — the adult equivalent of a child safeguarding practice review
  • Independent Mental Capacity Advocate — for those lacking capacity with no one to represent them
  • Links to the Mental Capacity Act / DoLS, the Mental Health Act, the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, and Deprivation of Liberty processes
Exam Pearls
What it is
Protecting an adult’s right to live free from abuse/neglect; Care Act 2014.
Section 42 duty
All 3: (1) care & support needs + (2) experiencing/at risk of abuse or neglect + (3) unable to protect themselves as a result.
Six principles
Empowerment, Prevention, Proportionality, Protection, Partnership, Accountability.
Key difference
“Making Safeguarding Personal” — work WITH the adult; a capacitous adult can decline help (right to unwise decisions). The key difference from child protection.
Abuse types
10 types; commonest = neglect/omission; financial abuse especially in elders; self-neglect now included.
Capacity is the hinge
Has capacity → consent needed (override only if risk to others / serious crime / coercion / public interest); lacks capacity → best interests (± Independent Mental Capacity Advocate).
Referral
Refer on reasonable suspicion, not proof; document + body map; consider others at risk.
Info sharing / machinery
Consent first, but share without it if incapacity / risk to others / public interest. Safeguarding Adults Board oversees; Safeguarding Adults Review = learning review after death/serious harm from suspected abuse/neglect.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Falls Assessment & P:
What & Why

A fall is an event where a person unintentionally comes to rest on the ground or a lower level. Falls are the defining “geriatric giant” — extremely common (around a third of over-65s fall each year) — and they matter because they cause fractures (especially hip), head injury, “long lie” complications, loss of confidence, functional decline, and loss of independence. The job is twofold: work out WHY this person fell (it’s almost never one thing) and reduce the risk of the next one — a fall is both an injury to treat and a red flag for underlying illness.

The framing that matters: falls are multifactorial. You don’t look for the cause — you find all the contributing factors and modify as many as you can. A fall in an older person is a syndrome, not a diagnosis, and is frequently the presenting sign of an acute illness (sepsis, MI, stroke, delirium) — “off legs” or a fall can be how pneumonia or a UTI shows up in the elderly.
Currency note: in April 2025, NICE replaced the long-standing CG161 with NG249. Two headline changes: it now covers people aged 50–64 at higher risk (not just ≥65), and it advises AGAINST using falls-risk-prediction tools (they lack sensitivity/specificity) — instead identify and act on individual risk factors. (Your exams may still reference CG161.)
The Decisive Question — a Fall, or a “Collapse”?
📷 Image placeholder — Mechanical/multifactorial fall vs syncope — the red flags (LOC, palpitations, exertional/chest symptoms, no memory) that divert to the TLoC/cardiac pathway

The first fork is distinguishing a mechanical/multifactorial fall from syncope (transient loss of consciousness) — a blackout points to a cardiac or neurological cause needing its own workup:

Mechanical / multifactorial fallSyncope / collapse
ConsciousnessNo loss of consciousness — tripped, legs gave way, lost balanceTransient loss of consciousness
CauseGait/balance, environment, meds, visionCardiac (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis), vasovagal, postural hypotension, neurological
WorkupMultifactorial falls assessmentECG, lying/standing BP, cardiac + transient-loss-of-consciousness pathway
Always ask about loss of consciousness — an unwitnessed “fall” may be a syncopal blackout. Red flags (loss of consciousness, palpitations, exertional/chest symptoms, no memory of the fall) → the transient-loss-of-consciousness / cardiac pathway.
Causes & Risk Factors (the multifactorial list)
Intrinsic (the patient)
  • Gait, balance, and mobility problems; muscle weakness (lower-limb strength is one of the strongest predictors)
  • Previous falls (the best single predictor of future falls) and fear of falling
  • Postural (orthostatic) hypotension; vision impairment (cataracts, poor acuity, bifocals on stairs)
  • Cognitive impairment / dementia / delirium; neurological (stroke, Parkinson’s, peripheral neuropathy)
  • Cardiovascular (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis, carotid sinus hypersensitivity); foot problems / inappropriate footwear
  • Continence (rushing to the toilet, nocturia); frailty, sarcopenia, acute illness (infection, MI, metabolic); alcohol
Medications (“falls-risk-increasing drugs” / FRIDs) — a core modifiable factor
  • Sedatives/hypnotics, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants (psychotropics are the big culprits)
  • Antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates (→ postural drop)
  • Opioids, anticholinergics, antiepileptics
  • Polypharmacy itself (≥4 medications)
Extrinsic (the environment)
  • Home hazards — loose rugs, poor lighting, trailing cables, clutter, no grab rails, stairs, slippery floors, wet bathrooms
Assessment — the Multifactorial Falls Assessment
📷 Image placeholder — Lying/standing BP — supine ≥5 min then measure at 1 and 3 min standing; positive if systolic drop ≥20 mmHg and/or diastolic drop ≥10 mmHg
Guideline-verified — NICE NG249. Who gets one: any older person who presents after a fall, reports recurrent falls in the past year, or has gait/balance problems — ask all older patients routinely: “have you fallen in the past year?”
  • History of the fall(s): context, frequency, loss of consciousness, prodrome, injuries, “long lie”
  • Gait and balance — observe walking; tools like the Timed Up-and-Go and Turn 180° test help observe deficits (NICE: useful for observing gait/balance but not as risk-prediction scores)
  • Muscle strength and functional ability
  • Lying and standing blood pressure (postural hypotension: drop ≥20 mmHg systolic / ≥10 mmHg diastolic on standing)
  • Cardiovascular exam + ECG (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis; consider if syncope); vision; cognitive assessment (screen for delirium/dementia)
  • Medication review (identify and rationalise FRIDs — STOPP/START); feet and footwear; continence
  • Bone health / fracture risk (FRAX, osteoporosis — falls + weak bones = fractures); home hazard assessment (validated tool, usually occupational therapy); fear of falling and functional impact
  • Investigations as guided: FBC, U&E, calcium, glucose, TFTs, vitamin D, B12 (reversible contributors), ECG, and imaging for injury (X-ray, CT head if head injury/anticoagulated)
Management — Individualised, Multifactorial Intervention
Guideline-verified — NG249; the evidence points to acting on identified risk factors.
  • Strength and balance training — the intervention with the strongest evidence. Individually prescribed muscle-strengthening + balance programmes (Otago Exercise Programme, Tai Chi) reduce falls — the single most effective measure
  • Medication review — stop/reduce FRIDs (psychotropics, sedatives; rationalise antihypertensives)
  • Treat postural hypotension — review culprit drugs, hydration, slow position changes, compression, (rarely) fludrocortisone/midodrine
  • Vision — cataract surgery, correct refraction; caution with bifocals/varifocals on stairs
  • Home hazard assessment and modification (occupational therapy) — grab rails, lighting, remove rugs, non-slip mats; footwear and foot care (podiatry)
  • Cardiac — treat arrhythmia; pacing for carotid sinus hypersensitivity / certain bradyarrhythmias
  • Bone protection / fracture prevention — calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonates where indicated (assess with FRAX/DEXA)
  • Continence management; address fear of falling (confidence-building, falls services); multidisciplinary falls service / CGA; assistive devices (walking aids fitted/taught by physio) and alarms/telecare for those living alone
After a Fall — the Acute Assessment
  • A–E, treat injuries; look for fracture (especially neck of femur — shortened, externally rotated leg), head injury (especially if anticoagulated), and “long lie” complications — rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, pressure sores, hypothermia, hypostatic pneumonia, dehydration
  • Find the trigger: obs + sepsis screen, ECG, lying/standing BP, glucose, bloods, medication review, neuro exam — a fall may be the presentation of acute illness
  • Then move to the multifactorial assessment and secondary prevention
Exam Pearls
Multifactorial
Find and modify ALL contributing factors, not one cause. A fall is often the presentation of acute illness (sepsis, MI, delirium).
First fork
Mechanical fall vs syncope — always ask about loss of consciousness → transient-loss-of-consciousness/cardiac pathway if present.
Best predictor
Previous falls = best single predictor of future falls. Ask every older patient: “have you fallen in the past year?”
Assessment
Gait/balance (Timed Up-and-Go), lying/standing BP, vision, cognition, meds (FRIDs), feet/footwear, cardiac/ECG, continence, bone health, home hazards.
NG249 (2025)
Don’t use falls-risk-prediction tools; act on individual risk factors; now covers 50+ at higher risk.
Best intervention
Strength & balance training (Otago, Tai Chi) has the strongest evidence for prevention.
Modifiable
Medication review (FRIDs: benzos, antipsychotics, antihypertensives, opioids) + treat postural hypotension + home hazard assessment. Postural hypotension = drop ≥20 systolic / ≥10 diastolic on standing.
Complications / bones
“Long lie”: rhabdomyolysis/acute kidney injury, pressure sores, hypothermia, pneumonia. Falls + osteoporosis = fractures → always address bone protection (calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonates, FRAX).
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Hyperthermia / Hypot:
What & Why

Hyperthermia is a raised core body temperature from a failure of thermoregulation — the body’s heat load exceeds its ability to dissipate heat. This is fundamentally different from fever, where the hypothalamic set-point is deliberately raised (by pyrogens): in hyperthermia the set-point is normal but the body can’t shed heat. That distinction has a critical consequence — antipyretics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) do NOT work in hyperthermia; the treatment is physical cooling. It matters because severe hyperthermia (heat stroke) is a medical emergency with high mortality, and the elderly are especially vulnerable during heatwaves.

The framing that matters: the whole topic is “why is this person hot, and can they cool themselves?” Two big branches: environmental heat illness (heat exhaustion → heat stroke) and drug-induced/metabolic hyperthermia (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic/sympathomimetic toxicity, thyroid storm). The unifying emergency principle is rapid cooling + supportive care + treat the cause.
The Decisive Fork — Heat Exhaustion or Heat Stroke?

For environmental heat illness this is the pivotal distinction — and it turns on one thing: the central nervous system:

Heat exhaustionHeat stroke (emergency)
Core tempRaised, usually <40°C>40°C
Central nervous systemIntact (may feel unwell/faint but oriented)ALTERED — confusion, agitation, ataxia, seizures, coma
FeaturesSweating, thirst, headache, nausea, cramps, tachycardia, malaise+ central-nervous-system dysfunction, ± organ failure
Reversible?Yes, with rest/rehydration/coolingLife-threatening; multi-organ failure
The presence of neurological dysfunction (altered mental state) is what defines heat stroke and separates it from heat exhaustion. Hyperthermia + confusion = heat stroke until proven otherwise.
Heat Stroke — Two Types
Classic (non-exertional)Exertional
WhoElderly, chronically ill, very young, on culprit drugsYoung, fit — athletes, soldiers, labourers
TriggerHeatwave / hot environmentStrenuous exertion in heat
SweatingOften absent (dry, hot skin)Often still sweating (a classic trap)
Key associationSocial isolation, immobilityRhabdomyolysis (very common), acute kidney injury
MortalityHigher (comorbid, elderly)Lower if cooled fast

Risk factors: extremes of age, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, antihistamines, diuretics, beta-blockers, stimulants/sympathomimetics, alcohol, dehydration, obesity, cardiovascular disease, immobility/social isolation, lack of air-conditioning.

Clinical Features & Complications of Heat Stroke
  • Core temp >40°C + central-nervous-system dysfunction (confusion → seizures → coma)
  • Tachycardia, hypotension (may mimic septic shock), tachypnoea
  • Complications: rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS, electrolyte derangement, multi-organ failure
  • Dark urine after exertion in heat = classic rhabdomyolysis clue
Investigations
  • Core (rectal) temperature — essential and continuous
  • Bloods: U&E, creatine kinase (rhabdomyolysis), LFTs, coagulation/DIC screen, FBC, glucose, ABG, lactate
  • Urinalysis (myoglobinuria), ECG
  • Rule out mimics — sepsis (culture), and consider the drug-induced syndromes from the history
Management — Heat Stroke
Guideline-verified — rapid cooling is everything.
The priorities
  • RAPID COOLING is the single most important, life-saving action — begin immediately, don’t wait for tests. Goal: core temp <39–40°C within ~30 minutes
  • Exertional heat stroke (young): cold/ice-water immersion is the most effective method (near-zero fatality if done fast)
  • Classic heat stroke (elderly): evaporative cooling (spray tepid water + fans) ± ice packs to groin/axillae/neck — better tolerated in frail patients. Stop cooling around 38.5–39°C to avoid overshoot
  • Antipyretics (paracetamol/NSAIDs) are INEFFECTIVE and potentially harmful (hepatic/renal) — do NOT use them
  • A–E resuscitation: oxygen, IV fluids (crystalloid) for hypotension/rhabdomyolysis, airway protection if reduced consciousness
  • Treat complications: aggressive fluids ± urinary alkalinisation for rhabdomyolysis/acute kidney injury, manage DIC, control seizures with benzodiazepines
  • Manage shivering/agitation (benzodiazepines) — shivering generates heat; avoid physical restraints (struggling generates heat). ICU for severe/multi-organ failure
  • Heat exhaustion: move to a cool place, rest, oral/IV rehydration, remove excess clothing, cool — recognise and treat before it progresses to heat stroke
The Hyperthermia Syndromes — the Key Differential

These mimic heat stroke but have specific triggers and antidotes — distinguishing them is classic exam material:

SyndromeTriggerOnsetDistinctive featuresSpecific treatment
Heat strokeEnvironmental heat/exertion—Hot dry (classic) skin, central-nervous-system dysfunctionCooling + supportive
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeAntipsychotics (or dopamine withdrawal)Slow (days)“Lead-pipe” rigidity, bradyreflexia, ↑↑creatine kinase, autonomic instabilityStop drug; dantrolene, bromocriptine
Serotonin syndromeSerotonergic drugs (SSRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid)Fast (hours)Clonus, hyperreflexia (especially lower limbs), agitation, dilated pupils, diarrhoeaStop drug; benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine
Malignant hyperthermiaVolatile anaesthetics + suxamethonium (RYR1 mutation)Minutes–hours of anaesthesiaMasseter/generalised rigidity, ↑↑↑CO2, ↑↑creatine kinase, hyperkalaemiaDantrolene (+ stop agent)
Anticholinergic toxicityAntimuscarinicsVariable“Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, blind as a bat” — dry skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, no rigiditySupportive; cooling; (physostigmine select)
Thyroid stormThyrotoxicosis + trigger—AF, tremor, goitre, thyroid historyBeta-blocker, propylthiouracil, iodine, steroids
Quick discriminators: rigidity + antipsychotic + slow onset = neuroleptic malignant syndrome; clonus/hyperreflexia + serotonergic drug + fast onset = serotonin syndrome; anaesthetic + rigidity + rising CO2 = malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene; dry, flushed, dilated pupils, no rigidity = anticholinergic.
Prevention (public-health / geriatric angle)

During heatwaves: hydration, cool environment/shade, avoid peak heat, light clothing, check on isolated elderly and those on culprit drugs, review diuretics/anticholinergics, and public Heat-Health alerts.

Exam Pearls
Not fever
Hyperthermia = normal set-point, failed heat loss → antipyretics DON’T work; cool physically.
Exhaustion vs stroke
Heat exhaustion (central nervous system intact, <40°C) vs heat STROKE (>40°C + ALTERED consciousness = emergency). Hyperthermia + confusion = heat stroke.
Two types
Classic = elderly, heatwave, dry skin; exertional = young athlete, often still sweating, + rhabdomyolysis.
Cooling
Rapid cooling is the life-saving priority — ice-water immersion (exertional) / evaporative cooling (elderly); target <39–40°C in ~30 min.
Complications
Rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury, DIC, hepatic failure. Check creatine kinase, coagulation, U&E, LFTs.
Differentials
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (antipsychotic, rigidity, slow → dantrolene/bromocriptine); serotonin syndrome (SSRI, clonus/hyperreflexia, fast → benzos/cyproheptadine); malignant hyperthermia (anaesthetic → dantrolene); anticholinergic (dry, no rigidity).
Geriatric point
Elderly on anticholinergics/antipsychotics/diuretics are high-risk in heatwaves.
What & Why

Hypothermia is a core body temperature below 35°C, from heat loss exceeding heat production. It matters as the thermoregulatory mirror-image of hyperthermia, as a classic geriatric and environmental emergency (the frail, isolated, immobile elderly are hit hardest — often indoors, in winter, after a fall and “long lie”), and because it carries two counterintuitive, high-yield rules: (1) “no one is dead until they’re warm and dead” — continue resuscitation through rewarming because the cold heart may be viable, and (2) handle gently and rewarm the core first — rough handling or peripheral rewarming can precipitate a fatal arrhythmia or afterdrop.

The framing that matters: hypothermia is graded by severity (temperature), and both the clinical picture and the rewarming strategy step up with each grade. The dangerous zone is <30°C, where the myocardium becomes electrically unstable and prone to ventricular fibrillation — which is why everything below that point is about minimal handling and careful, staged rewarming.
The Decisive Fork — How Cold? (staging)
📷 Image placeholder — Hypothermia stages by core temp — mild 32–35°C (shivering), moderate 28–32°C (shivering stops, bradycardia, Osborn waves), severe <28°C (VF/asystole risk), with rewarming stepping up per stage

Severity dictates the clinical picture and the rewarming method:

StageCore tempClinical pictureRewarming
Mild32–35°CShivering (present — a good sign), tachycardia, tachypnoea, vasoconstriction, confusion, ataxia, “cold diuresis”Passive external ± active external
Moderate28–32°CShivering STOPS, bradycardia, reduced consciousness, dilated pupils, Osborn (J) waves, AF, hyporeflexiaActive external + core
Severe<28°CComa, areflexia, fixed dilated pupils, hypotension, ventricular fibrillation/asystole risk, may appear deadActive internal core (± ECMO)
Shivering is a favourable sign — it means the patient is still mild (>~32°C) and generating heat. When shivering stops, they’ve dropped into the dangerous moderate/severe range.
Causes & Risk Factors
  • Environmental exposure — cold weather, immersion, inadequate clothing/heating
  • Elderly — impaired thermoregulation, immobility, social isolation, poverty/cold housing, a fall + long lie
  • Reduced heat production — hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism, hypoglycaemia, malnutrition, sepsis (can cause hypo- rather than hyperthermia in the elderly/immunosuppressed)
  • Impaired awareness/behaviour — alcohol (vasodilatation + impaired judgement), drugs/sedatives, dementia, reduced consciousness
  • Autonomic/skin — extensive burns, erythroderma; spinal injury. Neonates — large surface-area-to-volume ratio
Clinical Features

Progressive with cooling: shivering → confusion/ataxia/slurred speech → drowsiness → bradycardia, hypotension → coma, areflexia, ventricular fibrillation/asystole. “Paradoxical undressing” (removing clothes due to a confused sensation of warmth) is a recognised feature of severe hypothermia. Cold diuresis causes hypovolaemia.

Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — ECG in hypothermia — the Osborn (J) wave, a positive deflection at the J point (QRS–ST junction) that grows as core temperature falls; do not mistake for STEMI
  • Core (low-reading) temperature — a standard thermometer won’t read low enough; use a rectal/oesophageal low-reading probe
  • ECG — the key one: Osborn (J) wave — a positive deflection at the J point (QRS–ST junction), whose size correlates with the degree of hypothermia (invariably present <30°C). Also bradycardia, prolonged PR/QRS/QT, AF, and the classic sequence sinus bradycardia → AF → ventricular fibrillation → asystole. Don’t mistake Osborn waves for a STEMI
  • Bloods: glucose, U&E (acute kidney injury, potassium — a potassium >12 predicts non-survival and guides stopping resuscitation), TFTs (hypothyroidism), FBC, coagulation, blood gas, creatine kinase (rhabdomyolysis), amylase, cultures (sepsis), alcohol/toxicology
Management
Guideline-verified — Resuscitation Council UK / Advanced Life Support modifications.
General principles
  • A–E, minimal handling — rough movement can precipitate ventricular fibrillation in the cold, irritable heart. Move gently; avoid unnecessary procedures
  • Remove wet clothing, insulate, warm environment; warmed humidified oxygen; warmed IV fluids for the hypovolaemia of cold diuresis
  • Rewarm the core/trunk BEFORE the extremities — peripheral rewarming causes “afterdrop” (vasodilated cold limbs return cold, acidotic blood to the core → further temperature drop + hypotension)
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring; treat the underlying cause (hypothyroidism, sepsis, hypoglycaemia)
Rewarming methods (matched to severity)
  • Passive external (mild): remove wet clothes, blankets, warm room — aim ~0.5–2°C/hour
  • Active external (moderate): forced warm air (Bair Hugger), heating blankets, warm packs to trunk (not limbs)
  • Active internal / core (severe): warmed humidified oxygen, warmed IV fluids, body-cavity lavage (peritoneal/pleural), and — for severe/arrested/refractory — extracorporeal rewarming (ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass), the most effective
Cardiac arrest in hypothermia — key Advanced Life Support modifications
  • “No one is dead until warm and dead” — continue CPR through rewarming; a cold brain tolerates arrest far longer
  • Below ~30°C: the heart may be unresponsive to drugs and defibrillation — withhold arrest drugs, and limit defibrillation to 3 shocks until core temp rises above ~30°C
  • 30–35°C: double the interval between drug doses (slowed metabolism → accumulation)
  • Confirm death only after rewarming — fixed dilated pupils and rigidity are NOT reliable signs in hypothermia. Consider ECMO transfer for arrested/severe cases
Complications

Ventricular arrhythmias, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis/acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, coagulopathy/DIC, afterdrop, and frostbite / cold injury to extremities.

Exam Pearls
Staging
Core temp <35°C; mild 32–35 / moderate 28–32 / severe <28.
Shivering
Present = mild (good sign); shivering STOPS in moderate/severe.
ECG
Osborn (J) wave (positive deflection at the J point; size ∝ severity) + bradycardia, prolonged intervals, AF; arrhythmia sequence brady → AF → ventricular fibrillation → asystole. Don’t confuse with STEMI.
Handling
Handle gently — rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation.
Rewarming
Rewarm the CORE/trunk first — peripheral rewarming → “afterdrop.” Passive external (mild) → active external, e.g. Bair Hugger (moderate) → active internal/core ± ECMO (severe).
Resuscitation
“No one is dead until warm and dead” — continue CPR through rewarming. <30°C: withhold arrest drugs, max 3 shocks; 30–35°C: double drug intervals.
Causes / practical
Elderly + long lie, hypothyroidism, hypoglycaemia, sepsis, alcohol. Use a low-reading thermometer; cold diuresis → hypovolaemia (give warmed fluids).
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Malnutrition:
What & Why

Malnutrition (here meaning under-nutrition — a deficiency of energy, protein, and micronutrients) is a common, under-recognised, and reversible driver of poor outcomes in older people. It matters because it is hugely prevalent in the frail and hospitalised elderly, because it feeds directly into the geriatric syndromes — it drives sarcopenia → frailty → falls, impairs wound healing and immune function, and worsens recovery — and because it is both easy to screen for (MUST) and treatable (“food first”), yet routinely missed. It carries one high-yield danger: correcting it too fast causes refeeding syndrome.

The framing that matters: malnutrition in the elderly is a downstream marker of something else — you rarely find it in isolation. Someone is malnourished because of poor dentition, dysphagia, depression, dementia, social isolation, poverty, chronic disease, or the anorexia of ageing. So the task is screen → identify the cause → support intake (“food first”) → escalate if needed → and do it safely (watch for refeeding). It is a natural extension of Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment.
The Decisive Fork — Is This Person at Risk of Refeeding Syndrome?

Before you feed a malnourished patient, this is the safety question that changes everything:

Standard nutritional supportHigh refeeding risk
WhoMalnourished but adequately fed recentlyProlonged undernutrition / very low intake
ApproachOptimise intake toward requirementsStart LOW and SLOW, correct electrolytes, give thiamine, monitor
Danger—Refeeding syndrome (fatal shifts)
Causes & Risk Factors
  • Reduced intake: poor appetite (“anorexia of ageing”), depression, dementia, poor dentition/ill-fitting dentures, dysphagia (stroke, Parkinson’s), altered taste/smell, nausea
  • Social: isolation, bereavement, immobility, poverty (“heat or eat”), inability to shop/cook, reliance on carers
  • Increased requirements/losses: acute illness, cancer, chronic disease (COPD, heart failure, CKD), infection, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD, pancreatic), hyperthyroidism, surgery/wounds
  • Iatrogenic: polypharmacy (nausea, dry mouth, anorexia), nil-by-mouth episodes, restrictive diets
Recognition & Screening — MUST
📷 Image placeholder — MUST 5-step scoring — BMI (0/1/2) + unplanned weight loss over 3–6 months (0/1/2) + acute-disease effect (+2), summed to low/medium/high risk
Guideline-verified — NICE CG32/QS24, BAPEN. Screen all patients on hospital admission, GP registration, and when clinically concerned; rescreen weekly (inpatients).
MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool) — the validated UK 5-step tool; scores three components
  • BMI (0 = >20; 1 = 18.5–20; 2 = <18.5)
  • Unplanned weight loss over 3–6 months (0 = <5%; 1 = 5–10%; 2 = >10%)
  • Acute disease effect — add 2 if acutely ill and no/likely no nutritional intake for >5 days
  • Total: 0 = low risk (rescreen), 1 = medium risk (observe/food diary), ≥2 = high risk (treat — dietitian, nutrition plan)

Clinical signs: weight loss, loose clothing/dentures/rings, muscle wasting (temporal, thenar), sarcopenia, poor wound healing, fatigue, low mood, recurrent infection.

Assessment
  • Confirm and find the cause: dietary history, weight trend, dentition, swallow (SALT if dysphagia suspected), mood/cognition screen, social/functional review, drug review
  • Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFTs, phosphate, magnesium, potassium (baseline + for refeeding risk), calcium, glucose, CRP, albumin (a marker of illness/inflammation, not a reliable nutritional marker), vitamin D, B12/folate, ferritin, TFTs, coeliac serology if indicated
  • The GLIM criteria and EWGSOP2 sarcopenia assessment are increasingly used to formally diagnose malnutrition/sarcopenia
Management — the Escalation Ladder
📷 Image placeholder — Nutrition escalation ladder — food fortification → oral nutritional supplements → enteral (NG/PEG) → parenteral, with the trigger to step up at each rung
Guideline-verified — NICE CG32 / Malnutrition Pathway.
1. “Food First” — the foundation
  • Food fortification (add cream, butter, cheese, milk powder, oils to normal food to boost energy/protein density)
  • Small, frequent, energy-dense meals + nourishing snacks; nourishing drinks (full-fat milk, milky drinks)
  • Address the barriers: dentures/dental care, texture-modified diet for dysphagia (SALT-guided), assistance/adapted cutlery, social mealtimes, treat depression, manage nausea, review culprit drugs
2–4. Escalation if food-first is insufficient
  • Oral Nutritional Supplements (ONS) — only when “food first” fails (e.g. Ensure, Fortisip) for those malnourished or at risk; prescribed against ACBS indications, reviewed regularly
  • Enteral tube feeding (NG tube; PEG if long-term) — if the gut works but oral intake is unsafe/inadequate (e.g. stroke dysphagia). A best-interests/ethical decision in advanced dementia / end-of-life — tube feeding does NOT improve outcomes in advanced dementia and is generally not recommended; comfort/hand feeding is preferred
  • Parenteral nutrition — only if the gastrointestinal tract is non-functional/inaccessible (obstruction, short bowel, ileus). Carries infection/line risks
  • Dietitian and MDT throughout; monitor weight, intake, and biochemistry
Refeeding Syndrome — the Key Danger
What: in a chronically starved patient, reintroducing carbohydrate → surge of insulin → cells rapidly take up phosphate, potassium, magnesium, glucose, plus thiamine consumption → dangerous falls in serum phosphate/potassium/magnesium and fluid shifts → arrhythmias, cardiac/respiratory failure, seizures, Wernicke’s, death. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark.
High-risk criteria (NICE)
  • One or more of: BMI <16; unintentional weight loss >15% in 3–6 months; little/no intake >10 days; low potassium/phosphate/magnesium before feeding
  • OR two or more of: BMI <18.5; weight loss >10% in 3–6 months; little/no intake >5 days; history of alcohol misuse or drugs (insulin, chemo, antacids, diuretics)
Prevention / management
  • Start feeding LOW and SLOW — maximum ~10 kcal/kg/day, building up over ~4–7 days (5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases, e.g. BMI <14)
  • Give thiamine + vitamin B complex + multivitamins BEFORE and during feeding (prevents Wernicke’s)
  • Monitor and replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium daily; monitor fluid balance and ECG
Exam Pearls
What it is
Under-nutrition; common, reversible, under-recognised; drives sarcopenia → frailty → falls, poor wound healing, worse recovery.
Marker
It’s a marker of an underlying cause — dementia, depression, dysphagia, poor dentition, social isolation, chronic disease.
Screening
MUST (BMI + unplanned weight loss + acute-illness/no-intake >5d); score ≥2 = high risk.
Albumin
Albumin is NOT a reliable nutritional marker (it reflects inflammation).
Ladder
FOOD FIRST (fortification, snacks, address barriers) → ONS (only if food first fails) → enteral (NG/PEG) → parenteral (only if gut unusable).
Dementia
Tube feeding is NOT recommended in advanced dementia (no benefit; best-interests/comfort feeding).
Refeeding
Refeeding a starved patient → insulin surge → ↓↓phosphate (hallmark), ↓potassium, ↓magnesium → arrhythmias/death. High risk if BMI <16 / weight loss >15% / no intake >10d / low electrolytes (or two lesser criteria).
Prevent refeeding
Start low & slow + THIAMINE first + replace electrolytes.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Neck of Femur (NOF):
What & Why

A neck of femur (hip) fracture is the defining orthogeriatric emergency — a fragility fracture in a frail older person that is simultaneously an orthopaedic problem (fix the bone) and a whole-person medical crisis. It matters because it is common and lethal — around 10% die within 30 days and up to a third within a year — and because outcomes depend far more on the peri-operative medical care than on the operation itself. It is the model of integrated orthopaedic–geriatric (“orthogeriatric”) care.

The framing that matters: a hip fracture is not just a broken bone — it’s a sentinel event of frailty. The fracture will be fixed, but the patient dies of the complications — delirium, pneumonia, pressure sores, VTE, deconditioning. So peri-operative care is about protecting the whole patient through the insult of surgery and launching rapid rehabilitation, coordinated by a shared-care orthogeriatric team.
The Decisive Fork — Which Fracture, Driving Which Operation
