📷 Image placeholder — Intracapsular (subcapital/transcervical, above the capsule — retrograde supply disrupted → AVN risk → replace: THR/hemiarthroplasty) vs extracapsular (intertrochanteric → DHS; subtrochanteric/reverse-oblique → IM nail)

The anatomy (relative to the hip joint capsule) dictates the operation, because of the retrograde blood supply to the femoral head:

IntracapsularExtracapsular
LocationFemoral head → capsule insertionBelow capsule (inter-/sub-trochanteric)
Blood supply riskHigh avascular-necrosis risk (retrograde supply disrupted)Head supply intact
UndisplacedInternal fixation (or hemiarthroplasty if unfit)Dynamic hip screw (DHS) (stable inter-trochanteric)
DisplacedReplace the joint — total hip replacement or hemiarthroplastyIntramedullary nail (reverse-oblique/transverse/sub-trochanteric)
Garden classification (I–IV: incomplete → complete undisplaced → partially → fully displaced). Total hip replacement is favoured (over hemiarthroplasty) for a displaced intracapsular fracture if the patient walked independently outdoors (± a stick), is not cognitively impaired, and is medically fit. Signs: pain, shortened + externally rotated leg; X-ray shows a disrupted Shenton’s line.
Pre-operative Care
Guideline-verified — NICE CG124.
Immediate (emergency department / on admission)
  • A–E, resuscitation; treat what caused the fall (often a presentation of acute illness — sepsis, MI, arrhythmia, stroke, delirium)
  • Analgesia — early and cognition-sparing: assess pain immediately, paracetamol first-line/regular; consider a fascia iliaca compartment block (NICE recommends nerve blocks to supplement/spare opioids — reduces delirium, respiratory depression, constipation). Minimise opioids; avoid NSAIDs in the elderly (renal/GI)
  • Bloods, ECG, CXR, group & save; X-ray, and MRI (or CT) if occult fracture suspected with a normal X-ray
  • IV fluids, treat anaemia, correct reversible medical issues — but do NOT delay surgery for minor/uncorrectable abnormalities
  • Pressure area care from arrival; VTE assessment (mechanical prophylaxis; pharmacological per local protocol around surgery timing)
Timing of surgery
  • Operate on the day of, or the day after, admission — within ~36 hours, on a planned trauma list (the single most important peri-operative target; delay worsens mortality, delirium, and pressure sores)
  • Acceptable (correctable) reasons to delay: severe anaemia, uncontrolled heart failure, significant electrolyte/coagulation abnormality, uncontrolled diabetes, chest infection needing treatment
  • NOT acceptable: waiting for anticoagulation to wear off unnecessarily, minor derangements, “out of hours”
Orthogeriatric Shared Care
  • Admit under a formal orthogeriatric / shared-care pathway with early (≤72 h) comprehensive geriatric assessment
  • The geriatrician and orthopaedic team jointly manage the patient throughout — pre-op optimisation, medical co-morbidity, post-op complications, and rehab planning
  • This model reduces mortality, length of stay, and complications
Anaesthesia & Surgery
  • Spinal or general anaesthesia — either is acceptable; evidence shows no clear superiority of spinal over general for survival or recovery (a common misconception that spinal is always better)
  • Operate to allow immediate full weight-bearing where the fixation permits (dynamic hip screw/arthroplasty allow early mobilisation)
Post-operative Care & Rehabilitation
  • Mobilise the day after surgery (physiotherapy), then at least daily — central to preventing deconditioning, VTE, pneumonia, and pressure sores
  • Multidisciplinary rehabilitation — the Hip Fracture Programme (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, dietitian, nursing, orthogeriatrics), goal-oriented, aiming to return the patient to their pre-fracture residence and function
  • Analgesia to enable mobilisation; continue VTE prophylaxis
  • Delirium — screen (4AT), prevent, and treat proactively (very common post-hip-fracture)
  • Nutrition — screen (MUST), supplement; malnutrition impairs healing. Continence, skin/pressure care, catheter avoidance, bowel care
Bone health & falls — secondary prevention (don’t miss this)
  • Fracture prevention: assess and treat osteoporosis — calcium + vitamin D, and a bisphosphonate (this fracture is the diagnosis of osteoporosis; arrange DEXA/FRAX and bone protection)
  • Falls assessment — a hip fracture is a fall until proven otherwise; do a multifactorial falls assessment
Complications to Anticipate
  • Medical: delirium (very common), pneumonia/chest infection, VTE (DVT/PE), pressure ulcers, acute kidney injury, UTI, constipation, deconditioning/functional decline, and death
  • Surgical: avascular necrosis (intracapsular), non-union, infection, dislocation/failure of implant, peri-prosthetic fracture
Exam Pearls
What it is
Fragility fracture in a frail elder; ~10% 30-day mortality; a whole-person orthogeriatric emergency, not just a bone.
Operation
Intracapsular displaced → replace the joint (total hip replacement if fit/mobile/not cognitively impaired, else hemiarthroplasty) — avascular-necrosis risk from retrograde blood supply. Extracapsular: DHS (stable inter-trochanteric) / intramedullary nail (reverse-oblique/sub-trochanteric).
Signs
Shortened + externally rotated leg; disrupted Shenton’s line; Garden I–IV.
Timing
Operate within ~36 hours (day of/after admission) — don’t delay for minor/uncorrectable issues.
Analgesia
Early analgesia + fascia iliaca block to spare opioids and reduce delirium.
Shared care
Formal orthogeriatric shared care + comprehensive geriatric assessment within 72 h. Spinal vs general anaesthesia — no clear superiority.
Rehab
Mobilise day 1 post-op, daily multidisciplinary rehab, aim to return to pre-fracture function. Screen: delirium (4AT), VTE, pressure sores, malnutrition (MUST), constipation.
Secondary prevention
Osteoporosis treatment (calcium/vitamin D + bisphosphonate) + falls assessment — the fracture IS the osteoporosis diagnosis.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Polypharmacy (STOPP-:
What & Why

Polypharmacy is the concurrent use of multiple medications — commonly defined as ≥5 regular medicines — and it is one of the central problems of geriatric medicine. It matters because older, multimorbid patients accumulate drugs across decades and specialties, and each addition raises the risk of adverse drug reactions, interactions, falls, delirium, hospital admission, poor adherence, and ‘prescribing cascades’ (where a drug’s side-effect is treated with another drug). The STOPP/START criteria are the standard structured tool for tackling it — and the key move is that inappropriate prescribing runs in both directions.

The framing that matters: polypharmacy isn’t bad per se — a patient with several conditions may appropriately need several drugs. The problem is problematic (inappropriate) polypharmacy, and the goal isn’t to blindly cut pills but to optimise the regimen: stop what’s harmful/pointless (STOPP) and start what’s beneficial but missing (START). Deprescribing is an active, evidence-based clinical intervention, not neglect.
The Decisive Fork — Appropriate or Problematic Polypharmacy?
Appropriate polypharmacyProblematic polypharmacy
DefinitionMultiple drugs, each with a valid, current indication and net benefitDrugs that are unnecessary, harmful, duplicated, or whose harms outweigh benefits
ActionContinue + monitorStructured review → deprescribe / adjust
ExampleHeart-failure patient on ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker + diuretic (all indicated)A frail elder on a PPI “for years,” an anticholinergic causing falls, and a bisphosphonate near end of life
Why Older People Are Vulnerable
  • Pharmacokinetics: reduced renal clearance (↓eGFR → drug accumulation), altered hepatic metabolism, ↓ albumin (more free drug), altered body composition (↑ fat → longer half-life of lipophilic drugs like benzodiazepines)
  • Pharmacodynamics: increased sensitivity (e.g. to central-nervous-system depressants, anticholinergics, warfarin)
  • The frailty multiplier: reduced reserve → small drug effects cause big clinical harm (a sedative that’s trivial in a fit adult causes a fall/delirium in the frail)
Consequences of Problematic Polypharmacy
📷 Image placeholder — Prescribing cascade — amlodipine → ankle oedema → diuretic added → hypokalaemia/falls; a side-effect mistaken for a new diagnosis

Adverse drug reactions (a major cause of hospital admission in the elderly), falls, delirium, confusion, acute kidney injury, GI bleeding, prescribing cascades, poor adherence, drug interactions, and increased mortality and cost.

STOPP/START Criteria
📷 Image placeholder — STOPP (consider stopping: benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, anticholinergics, long-term full-dose PPI, NSAID in CKD/HF/on anticoagulant) vs START (consider starting: anticoagulant in AF, statin/ACEi/antiplatelet in CVD, bone protection post-fragility fracture)
Guideline-verified — STOPP/START version 3, 2023; the standard UK/European explicit tool.
STOPP — stop the harmful
  • Screening Tool of Older People’s Prescriptions
  • Flags Potentially Inappropriate Medications (PIMs) — drugs to consider stopping
START — start the missing
  • Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment
  • Flags Potential Prescribing Omissions (PPOs) — beneficial drugs that are missing and should be started
The key insight: inappropriate prescribing is bidirectional. Under-prescribing (a missed statin post-MI, no bone protection after a fragility fracture, no anticoagulation in AF) is as much an error as over-prescribing. Version 3 (2023) expanded to 190 criteria (from 114 in v2), with dedicated sections for falls-risk drugs, opioids, and anticholinergics. Using STOPP/START reduces adverse drug reactions, falls, and costs.
Common STOPP examples (consider stopping)
  • Benzodiazepines / Z-drugs, antipsychotics in those at risk of falls/confusion
  • Anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tricyclics, sedating antihistamines) — cognition, falls, retention, constipation
  • Long-term PPIs at full dose beyond indication
  • NSAIDs with CKD, heart failure, or on anticoagulants (GI bleed, acute kidney injury)
  • Duplicate drugs from the same class; digoxin at high dose in renal impairment; any drug with no evidence-based indication
Common START examples (consider starting)
  • Anticoagulation in AF (where indicated, no contraindication)
  • Statin / ACE inhibitor / beta-blocker / antiplatelet in established cardiovascular disease
  • Bone protection (bisphosphonate + calcium/vitamin D) after a fragility fracture
  • ACE inhibitor in heart failure / diabetic nephropathy
  • Inhaled therapy in documented COPD/asthma
Related tools
  • Anticholinergic Burden (ACB) score — quantifies cumulative anticholinergic load; higher burden → cognitive decline, falls, mortality. A key target for review
  • STOPPFrail (v2) — deprescribing criteria for frail older people with limited life expectancy (e.g. stopping statins/bisphosphonates near end of life)
  • Beers Criteria (US equivalent), Medication Appropriateness Index, NHS Scotland “7-Steps” review, NICE multimorbidity (NG56) guidance
Structured Medication Review — the Process
A patient-centred, systematic review — the “7-Steps” framework (NHS Scotland / NICE NG56)
  • Aim — what matters to the patient? (goals, life expectancy, values)
  • Identify essential drugs — don’t stop these
  • Does the patient take unnecessary drugs? — no indication, duplication, or the disease has resolved
  • Are therapeutic goals being achieved? — is each drug working and still needed?
  • Is there a safety problem? — adverse drug reactions, interactions, falls/anticholinergic burden, prescribing cascades
  • Cost-effectiveness — equally effective, cheaper alternatives
  • Is the patient willing and able? — shared decision-making, adherence, ability to manage
  • Shared decision with the patient/carer; explain the rationale
  • One change at a time where possible; taper drugs that need it (benzodiazepines, opioids, steroids, some antidepressants) to avoid withdrawal
  • Monitor for withdrawal effects or return of the condition; document and plan review
  • Match to goals of care — in advanced frailty/end of life, prioritise symptom control and quality of life; stop drugs with only long-term/preventive benefit (statins, bisphosphonates) whose payoff won’t be realised
Exam Pearls
What it is
Polypharmacy = ≥5 regular medicines; the problem is PROBLEMATIC (inappropriate) polypharmacy, not multiple drugs per se.
Vulnerability
Older people: ↓renal clearance, ↑sensitivity, frailty amplifies harm.
Bidirectional
STOPP = stop Potentially Inappropriate Medications; START = start beneficial omitted drugs — inappropriate prescribing is BIDIRECTIONAL.
Version 3
STOPP/START v3 (2023): 190 criteria, with falls / opioid / anticholinergic sections.
STOPP flags
Benzodiazepines/antipsychotics (falls), anticholinergics, long-term PPIs, NSAIDs in CKD/heart failure, duplicates.
START flags
Anticoagulation in AF, statin/ACE inhibitor/antiplatelet in cardiovascular disease, bone protection after fragility fracture.
Watch
Anticholinergic burden (ACB score) and prescribing cascades.
Review / deprescribe
7-Steps / NICE NG56: patient goals → essential drugs → unnecessary drugs → goals met? → safety → cost → adherence. Deprescribe: shared decision, one change at a time, taper where needed, monitor, match to goals of care (STOPPFrail near end of life).
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Pressure Sores:
What & Why

A pressure ulcer (pressure sore, decubitus ulcer, “bed sore”) is localised damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by sustained pressure — or pressure combined with shear. It matters because it is common, largely preventable, painful, costly, and a marker of care quality — and in the frail immobile elderly it drives infection, sepsis, prolonged admission, and death. It is also a safeguarding issue: an avoidable pressure ulcer can trigger an adult-safeguarding enquiry (neglect).

The framing that matters: the whole topic is “pressure + time + a vulnerable patient → tissue death,” and the clinical priority is overwhelmingly prevention over treatment. Identify who’s at risk, protect their skin relentlessly (the SSKIN bundle), and — if an ulcer develops — grade it, offload it, and manage the wound. Prevention is the answer to almost every exam question here.
The Mechanism

Sustained pressure over a bony prominence → occludes capillaries → local ischaemia → tissue hypoxia and necrosis. Contributing forces:

  • Pressure — the primary insult
  • Shear — tissue layers slide over each other (e.g. sliding down the bed) → deep vessel damage
  • Friction — surface rubbing → superficial breakdown
  • Moisture — incontinence/sweat macerates skin (moisture-associated damage — a related but distinct entity)

Common sites (over bony prominences): sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, elbows, occiput, malleoli. Also device-related (catheters, oxygen tubing, casts, nasogastric tubes) — an increasingly recognised category.

Risk Factors
  • Immobility (the biggest — bed/chair-bound, sedation, post-op, paralysis, “long lie”)
  • Reduced sensation (spinal injury, neuropathy, diabetes); impaired consciousness
  • Malnutrition & dehydration (impaired healing, thin subcutaneous padding)
  • Incontinence / moisture; poor perfusion (PVD, heart failure, hypotension, smoking)
  • Older age / frail thin skin, previous pressure ulcer, frailty and multimorbidity
Risk Assessment
Guideline-verified — NICE CG179.
  • Assume all patients are potentially at risk; formally assess those with risk factors, on admission and after any change in condition (surgery, deterioration, reduced mobility)
  • Validated tools support (don’t replace) clinical judgement: Waterlow score, Braden scale, or Norton scale; newer tools include PURPOSE-T
  • Skin assessment by a trained professional in high-risk patients — inspect for colour change (non-blanching erythema), pain, temperature/firmness/moisture changes
  • In darker skin tones, early damage may not appear as redness — look for purplish/bluish discolouration, and changes in temperature, firmness, or the patient reporting pain; palpate, don’t just look
Categorisation (EPUAP/NPIAP International Classification)
📷 Image placeholder — Pressure-ulcer categories — 1 (non-blanchable erythema, intact skin) → 2 (partial-thickness/blister) → 3 (full-thickness, subcutaneous fat) → 4 (bone/tendon/muscle exposed), plus unstageable (eschar-obscured) and deep tissue injury (maroon/purple)
CategoryDescription
Category 1Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin (redness that doesn’t blanch on pressure; in dark skin, discolouration/temperature change)
Category 2Partial-thickness skin loss — dermis exposed; shallow open ulcer or intact/ruptured blister
Category 3Full-thickness skin loss — subcutaneous fat visible; may have slough; muscle/bone NOT exposed
Category 4Full-thickness tissue loss — exposed bone, tendon, or muscle; often slough/eschar, undermining/tunnelling

Prevention — the SSKIN Bundle
SSKIN — the core prevention framework
  • S — Surface: appropriate pressure-redistributing mattress/cushion (high-spec foam for at-risk; dynamic/alternating-pressure surfaces for high-risk)
  • S — Skin inspection: regular skin checks, especially over bony prominences; keep clean and dry
  • K — Keep moving: reposition regularly — at-risk adults at least every 6 hours, high-risk at least every 4 hours; document the schedule; heel offloading
  • I — Incontinence/moisture: manage incontinence, barrier creams, keep skin dry
  • N — Nutrition/hydration: screen (MUST) and optimise protein/calorie/fluid intake
Do NOT massage or rub skin over bony prominences to prevent ulcers — it causes damage (a classic exam point; NICE says do not offer skin massage/rubbing to prevent a pressure ulcer).
Management of an Established Ulcer
  • Relieve the pressure — offload immediately (repositioning, appropriate support surface). Nothing heals under continued pressure
  • Categorise and document — site, category, size (measure/photograph), and progress; document surface area with a validated technique
  • Debridement of slough/necrotic tissue (autolytic dressings usually; sharp/surgical if needed) — but stable dry heel eschar is often left intact (protective) unless infection/instability
  • Dressings to maintain a moist wound environment (hydrocolloids, foams, alginates, hydrogels) matched to exudate; avoid routine gauze (adherent, painful). Manage exudate/odour
  • Infection: do NOT swab routinely (all ulcers are colonised); swab/treat only with clinical signs of infection (spreading erythema, heat, increasing pain, systemic upset, cellulitis, delayed healing). Systemic antibiotics for spreading infection/cellulitis/osteomyelitis/sepsis — not for colonisation; consider X-ray/MRI for suspected osteomyelitis
  • Nutrition optimisation (protein, vitamin C, zinc as needed), pain control; adjuncts: negative-pressure wound therapy for selected cavity wounds; tissue-viability/plastics referral for complex or category 3–4 ulcers
  • Consider safeguarding where an ulcer may reflect neglect (adult safeguarding referral)
Complications

Local/systemic infection — cellulitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis; chronic non-healing wounds; pain; fluid/protein loss; prolonged admission; rarely Marjolin’s ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in chronic wounds); death.

Exam Pearls
What it is
Localised skin/tissue damage over a bony prominence from sustained pressure ± shear → capillary occlusion → ischaemia.
Sites
Sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, trochanters, occiput. Watch device-related ulcers.
Risk
Biggest = immobility; also malnutrition, incontinence/moisture, poor perfusion, reduced sensation, frailty. Tools: Waterlow, Braden, Norton (support, don’t replace, judgement).
Dark skin
Look for discolouration + temperature/firmness/pain — not just redness.
Categories
1 = non-blanchable erythema (intact); 2 = partial-thickness (dermis); 3 = fat visible; 4 = bone/tendon/muscle exposed (+ unstageable + deep tissue injury).
Prevention
SSKIN: Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving (reposition ≥4–6-hourly), Incontinence/moisture, Nutrition. Do NOT massage bony prominences.
Management
OFFLOAD + categorise/document + moist wound dressings + debride (not stable heel eschar) + antibiotics only for clinical infection. Do NOT routinely swab.
Safeguarding
Avoidable pressure ulcer → consider adult safeguarding.
GERIATRIC MEDICINE__Frailty (Rockwood CF:
What & Why

Frailty is a distinct health state of reduced physiological reserve across multiple body systems, leaving a person disproportionately vulnerable to decompensation after a minor stressor event. It matters because it is the unifying concept of geriatric medicine — the thing that sits underneath falls, delirium, incontinence, and the whole rationale for Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. It predicts adverse outcomes better than age or any single diagnosis, and — crucially — it is not fixed: it can be identified, graded, and modified.

The framing that matters: the defining idea is the stressor–decompensation model. A minor event (a UTI, a new drug, a night in hospital) that a fit person shrugs off can, in a frail person, trigger a dramatic, disproportionate deterioration — a sudden fall in function that is slow (and sometimes incomplete) to recover. Frailty is why an older person presents with a “geriatric giant” (falls, immobility, delirium, incontinence) rather than the textbook features of the underlying illness.
The Decisive Fork — Which Model of Frailty?

There are two ways to conceptualise and measure frailty — know both and how they differ:

Fried phenotype — the 5 criteria
  • Unintentional weight loss (e.g. ≥4.5 kg/year)
  • Weakness (reduced grip strength)
  • Exhaustion (self-reported)
  • Slow walking speed
  • Low physical activity — ≥3 = frail; 1–2 = pre-frail; 0 = robust. Core feature = sarcopenia (the biological engine of physical frailty)
Rockwood cumulative deficit model
  • Frailty = the number of accumulated deficits (medical, functional, psychosocial)
  • Frailty Index = (deficits present) ÷ (deficits assessed); closer to 1.0 = frailer
  • Underpins the electronic Frailty Index (eFI) — auto-calculated from 36 deficits in GP records, used across ~95% of UK practices to identify frailty at scale
The Clinical Frailty Scale

Rockwood’s practical bedside scale — a 9-point clinical-judgement scale, scored after a holistic assessment, that maps a person’s baseline function (usually ~2 weeks before an acute illness) onto a level of frailty. It’s the workhorse in UK acute/emergency settings:

ScoreCategoryDescription
1Very fitRobust, active, energetic, exercise regularly
2Fit (well)No active disease but less fit than category 1
3Managing wellMedical problems well controlled, not regularly active
4Vulnerable (very mild frailty)Not dependent, but symptoms limit activities; “slowed up”
5Mildly frailNeeds help with IADLs (finances, transport, shopping, heavy housework)
6Moderately frailNeeds help with outside activities + some ADLs (bathing, dressing)
7Severely frailCompletely dependent for personal care; stable
8Very severely frailCompletely dependent, approaching end of life; wouldn’t recover from minor illness
9Terminally illLife expectancy <6 months, not otherwise evidently frail
Practical anchors: 1–3 = fit; 4 = vulnerable/pre-frail; 5–6 = mild–moderate frailty; 7–9 = severe. Score the BASELINE, not the acute state (function ~2 weeks before the current illness). Validated in adults ≥65 — don’t use in younger people or those with stable long-standing disability/learning disability.

Why it matters: it predicts mortality, length of stay, and outcomes; it guides escalation/ceiling-of-treatment decisions, resuscitation discussions, and eligibility for interventions (surgery, intensive care, thrombolysis pathways) — always alongside clinical judgement and the patient’s wishes, never as a sole determinant.

Other Identification Tools
  • Gait speed (>5 s to walk 4 m suggests frailty) and the timed up-and-go — quick, practical screens
  • PRISMA-7 questionnaire (≥3 suggests frailty)
  • FRAIL scale, Edmonton Frail Scale, Hospital Frailty Risk Score (from admin data)
Consequences of Frailty

Increased risk of falls, delirium, immobility, incontinence (the geriatric giants), fluctuating disability, iatrogenic harm/polypharmacy sensitivity, hospital admission, longer stays, institutionalisation, and death. Frailty is the reason older people have atypical presentations of illness.

Management
Guideline-verified — British Geriatrics Society.
  • Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment is the cornerstone — the multidimensional, MDT process that turns a frailty label into a coordinated plan
  • Exercise — the strongest-evidence intervention: progressive resistance (strength) + balance training improves muscle mass, function, and reduces falls
  • Nutrition — adequate protein and calories; treat malnutrition; address sarcopenia; correct vitamin D
  • Medication review — rationalise polypharmacy and stop falls-risk-increasing/anticholinergic drugs (STOPP/START)
  • Optimise chronic disease and treat reversible contributors (anaemia, thyroid, depression, sensory impairment); address the geriatric giants proactively
  • Advance care planning — frailty is the trigger for conversations about ceilings of care, ReSPECT, and preferences; social/community support (carers, care packages, telecare, falls services)
  • Frailty is dynamic — it can be stabilised or improved; the goal is maintaining/restoring function and independence, not just managing decline
Exam Pearls
What it is
Reduced physiological reserve across systems → disproportionate decompensation after a MINOR stressor. Why older people present with “geriatric giants,” not textbook disease.
Two models
Fried phenotype (5 physical criteria, ≥3 = frail; core = sarcopenia) vs Rockwood cumulative deficit (Frailty Index = deficits ÷ total, 0–1).
Fried 5
Weight loss, weakness (grip), exhaustion, slow gait, low activity.
Clinical Frailty Scale
9 points (1 very fit → 9 terminally ill); 1–3 fit, 4 vulnerable, 5–6 mild–moderate, 7–9 severe.
Scoring caveat
Score on BASELINE function (~2 weeks pre-illness), in adults ≥65 — not the acute state, not younger/stable-disability patients.
eFI
Electronic Frailty Index (36 deficits) in UK GP records — population-level identification.
Predicts / guides
Falls, delirium, admission, institutionalisation, death; guides (not dictates) escalation/ceiling-of-care decisions.
Management
Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment + strength/balance exercise (best evidence) + nutrition + medication review (STOPP/START) + advance care planning. Frailty is NOT fixed — it can be improved.
